title: Phillies land Luis Arraez, reliever from Giants in trade that will realign infield: Sources
author: Matt Gelb
content:
The Philadelphia Phillies turned to an outside-the-box solution to upgrade their offense by landing veteran second baseman Luis Arraez in a deadline-day trade Monday with the San Francisco Giants. It’s a move that brings a former batting champion into the lineup, but one that will prompt an infield realignment.

The Phillies, according to league sources who spoke on condition of anonymity because the deal was not completed, will also receive righty reliever Caleb Kilian. They are sending pitching prospects Ramon Marquez and Marty Gair to the Giants.

Arraez will play second base for the Phillies. Teams speaking to the Giants about Arraez were aware of his insistence on staying at second base. The Phillies made the trade regardless.

He is that big of an upgrade. Arraez, a three-time batting champ, is leading the league with a .324 average this season. He has an .801 OPS.

The Phillies, according to team sources, have several avenues they can now take. They could move Bryson Stott to third base, bump Alec Bohm to first base and return Bryce Harper to right field. Harper said last week he was willing to move back to the outfield if needed.

Harper, as of Sunday, said he had not discussed that possibility with team officials.

But there are other scenarios, those sources said. The Phillies could do less rearranging by keeping Harper at first base, moving only Stott to third base, and look to move Bohm in a trade later Monday.

They also could keep Harper and Bohm on the infield corners and send Stott to the outfield, an option the club has discussed internally.

Whatever path the Phillies follow, it’s a creative way to address the lackluster lineup. The Phillies needed a right-handed-hitting outfielder. They instead acquired a lefty-hitting second baseman.

Arraez, 29, entered this season as a .317 lifetime hitter and he’s contending for what would be his fourth batting title while playing in an era of hit suppression and plummeting averages. There’s no doubt he’s an outlier in today’s game. Yet it’s more difficult to determine the true value of his offensive skills, which is why the Giants were able to sign him to a modest one-year, $12 million contract.

It was San Francisco’s best move in an otherwise unsuccessful winter. Arraez has been a shining light in a dismal season and he’s rebuilt his defensive reputation at second base while ranking near the top of the list for all defenders in Outs Above Average and Fielding Run Value. He’s become an instant fan favorite with his feisty and competitive at-bats, too.

As an impending free agent, though, there wasn’t much doubt that the Giants would seek to move Arraez before the trade deadline. His elite bat-to-ball skills figured to be in high demand among contending clubs, especially after teams such as the Toronto Blue Jays and Milwaukee Brewers used high-contact lineups to churn through postseason opponents last October.

Arraez has the slowest average bat speed in the league, but that’s by design. His ultra-short swing allows him to wait till the last instant to make a swing decision, and then he keeps his bat in the zone for as long as it takes to make contact. He won’t draw walks, and nobody in the game is more geared to swing with two strikes — amazingly, he had just two called strikeouts in 675 plate appearances last season — but he’s the rare hitter who lacks power but is otherwise someone you want at the plate in an RBI situation.

Kilian, 29, is an enticing bullpen addition for the Phillies. He had eight career games in the majors before this season and spent an injury-riddled 2025 in the minors. But he is throwing harder than ever, averaging 97 mph with a fastball that has held opponents to a .296 slugging percentage. He has a 27 percent strikeout rate with a few too many walks, but he fits in the middle of the Phillies’ bullpen. He also has five years of club control remaining.

Marquez, who quickly established himself as one of the best pitchers in the Phillies’ system this season, highlights the return for the Giants.

The 20-year-old righty was widely viewed as one of the Phillies’ best pitching prospects. He has a strong changeup and his fastball velocity has improved since he came stateside last year. His ability to develop a strong breaking pitch remains a question mark; he throws a slider, but it’s his weakest pitch. Nonetheless, he has made a name for himself in just a year and a half since signing for $10,000 out of Mexico.

Gair, a 23-year-old righty reliever, was recently promoted to the Phillies’ High-A affiliate. He has posted a 4.50 ERA across 36 innings this season. Injuries have derailed much of his development, as he has only pitched 63 innings since being selected in the 13th round of the 2023 MLB Draft. But his fastball averaged nearly 98 mph in the Low-A Florida State League this year, where he struck out more than 40 percent of the batters he faced.
